title: Systems for Machine Learning
premise: The hardware reality underneath everything above, and the answer to a question the rest of the programme keeps raising without settling: why do modern architectures look the way they do. They look that way because of memory bandwidth. Attention is not slow because of its arithmetic — the arithmetic is cheap — it is slow because it moves more data than it computes on, and once that is a number you have measured rather than a claim you have read, half the design decisions in a modern model stop being arbitrary.
why_here: Thirteenth, after transformers, because the systems argument is only interesting once you know what is being computed. It also completes AIE-105 from the other end: that course optimised inference cost from the outside, treating the model as a service with a price. This one opens it.
laboratory: Free-tier hosted GPU, and honesty about the constraint. There is no GPU on this laptop and the droplet is a 1 vCPU box that is not a laboratory for anything. The profiling items run on a free Colab or Kaggle session; the arithmetic items — intensity, roofline, communication volume — need no accelerator at all and are done on paper and checked in numpy. Where an item genuinely needs hardware that is not free, it says so and gives a smaller substitute rather than pretending.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing. AIE-105 evidences cost accounting at the API boundary, which is the opposite side of this course's subject and tells you nothing about the memory hierarchy underneath it.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: Judges are instructed that measurements taken on a free-tier T4 are the intended scale, and that a submission must not be marked down for modest hardware where the rubric asks about mechanism, arithmetic or attribution.

FlashAttention, for the IO argument
items.locator: Read this time for the IO-complexity analysis rather than the algorithm. AIE-204 read it as an implementation detail; here the point is the counting of memory accesses that motivates it.

items.title: Measure the hierarchy yourself
checkpoints: A bandwidth-bound microbenchmark written and timed
A compute-bound microbenchmark written and timed
Achieved bandwidth and achieved FLOP/s computed from the timings
Both compared against the device's published specification
items.brief: Write two microbenchmarks on whatever accelerator you can get free: one that does almost no arithmetic per byte moved, and one that does a great deal. Time both, and convert the timings into achieved memory bandwidth and achieved FLOP/s. Compare each against the device's published numbers. You will not reach either figure, and the size of the shortfall — plus your explanation of it — is the assignment.

items.title: Attention's IO cost, from your own numbers
checkpoints: Bytes moved by a naive attention implementation counted analytically
FLOPs counted analytically for the same shapes
The ratio computed and compared against the device's ratio from M1.4
The prediction checked against a timed run
items.brief: Count, on paper, how many bytes a naive attention implementation moves and how many floating-point operations it performs, for a stated sequence length and head dimension. Take the ratio. Compare it against the bandwidth-to-compute ratio you measured in M1.4 and predict whether attention is memory-bound or compute-bound at that shape. Then time it and see whether your prediction held. Do this at two sequence lengths, because the answer changes with length and that is the whole point.

items.title: Four operations, predicted then measured
checkpoints: Arithmetic intensity derived by hand for four operations
A bound predicted for each, recorded before measuring
All four timed
Predictions scored against outcomes
items.brief: Take four operations — an elementwise activation, a layer normalisation, a small matrix multiply and a large one. Derive the arithmetic intensity of each by hand: operations per byte moved. Predict which are memory-bound and which are compute-bound, and write the predictions down before running anything. Then measure. Report how many you got right, including the ones you did not, because a wrong prediction traced to its cause teaches more than four correct ones.

items.title: A roofline for the hardware you actually have
checkpoints: Peak bandwidth and peak compute established empirically, not from the datasheet
The ridge point computed
The four operations from M2.2 plotted on it
One operation's position used to argue for a specific optimisation
items.brief: Build a roofline model for your available device using the peaks you measured rather than the ones the vendor advertises. Compute the ridge point — the arithmetic intensity above which you become compute-bound. Plot the operations from the previous assignment. Then use the plot to argue for one specific optimisation on one specific operation, and say what you expect it to buy before trying it.

items.title: Attribute every millisecond of a training step
checkpoints: A single training step profiled with a real profiler
Time attributed to forward, backward, optimiser and data loading
Kernel-level breakdown for the largest contributor
Unattributed time reported rather than absorbed
items.brief: Profile one training step of the model you built in AIE-204. Attribute the time: forward, backward, optimiser, data loading, and whatever is left. Break the largest contributor down to individual kernels. Report the unattributed remainder explicitly — profilers never account for everything, and a breakdown that sums to exactly 100% has been rounded into agreement.

items.title: One change, predicted before it is made
checkpoints: One optimisation chosen from the profile and the reason recorded
A quantitative prediction written down before the change
The change made and re-profiled
Prediction and outcome compared, with any gap explained
items.brief: Pick one optimisation the profile actually justifies — mixed precision, a fused optimiser, compilation, a larger batch — and predict the speedup quantitatively before making the change. Then make it and re-profile. Compare the prediction against the outcome. Getting the number wrong is expected; not being able to say why afterwards is the failure, and a prediction made after the measurement is not a prediction.

items.locator: The parallelism and distributed training lectures — the three strategies and the communication each one requires per step.

items.title: Switch Transformers, for the routing cost
Communication volume, by hand
checkpoints: A model size and cluster shape stated
Bytes communicated per step derived for data parallelism
The same for tensor and for pipeline parallelism
The three compared against a stated interconnect bandwidth
items.brief: Fix a model size and a cluster shape — eight devices, a stated parameter count, a stated batch. Derive how many bytes cross the interconnect per training step under data parallelism, under tensor parallelism, and under pipeline parallelism. Divide by a realistic interconnect bandwidth to get a time. You cannot run this, and you do not need to: the arithmetic is the deliverable, and it is what the strategy choice actually rests on.

items.title: Choose a strategy for a stated budget
checkpoints: A concrete scenario fixed — model size, hardware, budget, deadline
A strategy or combination chosen
The choice defended with the arithmetic from M4.3
The conditions that would flip the decision stated
items.brief: Given a concrete scenario — a model that does not fit on one device, a fixed number of GPUs, a budget and a deadline — choose a parallelism strategy or combination and defend it with your own communication arithmetic rather than by citing what a large lab did. Then state what would change your answer: a different interconnect, a different model shape, a smaller batch. A recommendation with no stated failure conditions is an opinion.

modules.title: Apply it to something you actually run

items.title: The systems view of your own inference path
checkpoints: One of your own products' inference paths described in systems terms
The bound identified for each stage — memory, compute, or network
AIE-105's cost and latency measurements reconciled with this view
One optimisation identified that the outside view could not see
items.brief: Take an inference path from one of your own products and describe it in the terms of this course: for each stage, is it bound by memory, by compute, or by the network between you and the provider. Reconcile that against the cost and latency numbers AIE-105 produced from the outside. The deliverable is one optimisation that only becomes visible from the systems view — and it is a legitimate outcome to conclude that for an API-backed product, the answer is that none of it is yours to optimise.

items.title: Publish the performance chapter
checkpoints: Written for a reader who has never profiled anything
The roofline and the profile both included and explained
At least one prediction that was wrong, kept in
Published and connected backwards to AIE-105 or AIE-204
items.brief: Publish a chapter covering what you measured and what it changed. Include a prediction you got wrong — they are the most instructive part of a performance write-up and the first thing most authors delete. It must connect backwards: AIE-105 measured cost from outside the model, AIE-204 built the thing being measured, and this chapter is what joins them.

items.title: Where the systems view changes an architecture choice
checkpoints: An architectural feature identified whose motivation is systems, not modelling
The memory or bandwidth argument for it reconstructed
What it would cost on a device with a different ratio, stated
items.brief: Pick a feature of modern architectures whose real motivation is hardware rather than modelling — grouped-query attention, the shape of a feed-forward layer, the choice of head dimension. Reconstruct the systems argument for it from your own measurements. Then state what would have to be true about a device for that feature to stop being worth it. This is the outcome the course exists for: architectures look the way they do because of the machines they run on, and being able to say which parts are which is rare.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own submissions at defense time, answered aloud without notes and without a calculator.
sample_question_shapes: Estimate, out loud, whether a layer normalisation on a batch of ten thousand rows is memory-bound or compute-bound. Show me the reasoning, not the answer.
Your predicted speedup was double what you measured. Where did the prediction go wrong?
Someone proposes tensor parallelism across eight machines on a slow interconnect. Talk them out of it, or into it, with numbers.

items.title: Quantisation and pruning
items.locator: The lectures on quantisation and on pruning — the two techniques that change the arithmetic-intensity picture rather than working within it.

completion.required: All eight assignments, the project and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the GPU execution model and distributed training, which sit in the inference area — so this course deepens a capability AIE-105 already made claimable rather than unlocking a new one. FSRS then decays them.
